newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: NATO's Solana given wary welcome in Central Asia.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana given wary welcome in Central Asia.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana told Kazakh deputies in far-flung Central Asia on Tuesday that an accord between Russia and the western alliance was essential for global security in the next century.

"A new NATO and a new Russia have to do their best to reach this agreement in order to enter the next century with better security conditions," Solana told members of both houses of parliament in the Kazakh capital Almaty.

Solana, at the start of a five-day tour of four Central Asian nations, must convince the ex-Soviet states that NATO's sparring with the Kremlin over the alliance's plans to expand eastwards does not threaten their own fragile stability.
Moscow and NATO are at loggerheads over the alliance's plans to invite in new members at a July summit in Madrid. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are favourites to be the first new entrants.
"For Kazakhstan, in principle, NATO expansion does not constitute any threat for its security," Kazakh Foreign Minister Kasymzhomart Tokayev told reporters.
But Tokayev added: "The process of expansion is inevitable but it is important to heed Russia's concerns."
Solana is officially touring Central Asia to discuss the participation of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan in NATO's "Partnership for Peace" programme.
The fifth former Soviet republic in Central Asia, Tajikistan, devastated by a four-year civil war and prey to a motley array of armed bands, is not on Solana's itinerary.
Solana's visit to other ex-Soviet republics in February prompted loud criticism from the Kremlin.

So this time Solana and the Central Asian republics have been at pains to stress NATO involvement in anything from fighting drug trafficking to environmental protection but have kept away from any any controversial defence issues.
"We can offer you technical assistance in many fields," Solana told deputies. NATO will carry out a 10-day peacekeeping exercise with Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan in September in the region.

Communist opposition deputy Valerian Zemlyanov was not convinced by Solana's softly-softly sales pitch. "We don't know the real goal of NATO," he said. "We can't stop NATO expansion, but we don't welcome it," he said.

Western diplomats say the visit is merely a courtesy call and that NATO has no long range plans to include the remote region of mountain, desert and steppe in the alliance. The main aim, they say, is to get Russia's neighbours on side.
Asked by a Kazakh deputy if Russia and the Central Asian states might one day join the alliance, Solana replied enigmatically: "Nothing is written, everything is possible."
